P1_fx_receipts.question: Can resident individuals receive foreign currency for services or digital exports? Any conversion or repatriation rule?
P1_fx_receipts.answer: No. As an EU member state, Germany applies Article 63 TFEU, which prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments between EU countries and with non-EU countries. Banks still apply AML/KYC checks and may ask for the source of funds.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and payments between EU countries, as well as between EU and non-EU countries.

P2_fcy_account.question: Can resident individuals hold a foreign-currency account locally?
P2_fcy_account.answer: Yes. Private customers can open a foreign-currency account (Fremdwährungskonto) at many German banks or online brokers (Finanztip). It is typically a sub-account of an existing settlement or current account; BNP Paribas Private Banking's opening form, for example, offers USD, GBP, CAD, AUD, JPY and other currencies (BNP Paribas). Some banks offer it only to existing customers. EU law (art. 63 TFEU) bars restrictions on capital movements.

sources.title: Free movement of capital (European Parliament Fact Sheet)
sources.quote: ensuring that payments in relation to those capital movements can be executed without restrictions, so that individuals and businesses can use, invest and/or save their money or financial assets anywhere within the EU as well as in non-EU countries.

L1_registration.question: Must an individual register a business to sell digital services/products? Simplest legal form?
L1_registration.answer: Freelancers (Freiberufler) do not need to register a business (Gewerbe) or enter the Commercial Register; they register with the local tax office (Finanzamt) by filing the tax registration questionnaire (Fragebogen zur steuerlichen Erfassung) via ELSTER, generally within one month of starting. Traders (Gewerbetreibende) also file a Gewerbeanmeldung with the municipality (not captured). The questionnaire is also where you opt into the small-business (Kleinunternehmer) VAT scheme.

L3_income_tax_foreign.question: Income tax on foreign-source income for residents; rates or special regimes
L3_income_tax_foreign.answer: Tax residents of Germany are taxed on worldwide income (see quoted rules for exceptions such as remittance-basis regimes). Progressive up to 45% plus solidarity surcharge (rates not captured). Inference (general source principle, not quoted): work performed while living in Germany for foreign clients is normally taxable in Germany.

L4_vat_gst.question: VAT/GST: rate, registration threshold, treatment of exported digital services
L4_vat_gst.answer: National threshold (Kleinunternehmerregelung, § 19 UStG, from 2025): no VAT is charged if total turnover was at most EUR 25,000 in the previous year and stays at most EUR 100,000 in the current year. In the founding year, the limit is EUR 25,000 of actual turnover, with no annualisation. Exceeding EUR 25,000 in a year means standard VAT from 1 January of the next year. Waiving the exemption binds you to standard taxation for five years. The standard VAT rate is 19%. Under the EU SME scheme, small businesses below a national threshold (at most EUR 85,000) can be exempt on domestic sales. Where services are taxed (EU-wide rules, illustrated by Irish Revenue guidance): (1) B2B, meaning services to business customers in other EU countries or outside the EU, are taxed where the customer is established, so no Germany VAT is charged; EU business customers self-account under the reverse charge. (2) B2C services to private individuals are, as a rule, taxed where the supplier is established, so Germany VAT applies once you are VAT-registered. (3) Exception: consultancy, legal, accounting, engineering, data-processing, advertising, licensing and electronically supplied services to private customers outside the EU are outside EU VAT, subject to 'use and enjoyment' rules. Electronically supplied services to private customers in other EU countries follow special OSS rules (not captured here).

L5_data_protection.question: Data-protection law applicable to a small online business
L5_data_protection.answer: The EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applies directly in Germany, supervised by the national data protection authority. It covers EU businesses and non-EU businesses offering goods or services to people in the EU.

sources.title: Data protection (European Commission)
sources.quote: EU data protection legislation is comprised of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Law Enforcement Directive (LED), and the Data Protection Regulation for EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies (EUDPR).

sources.title: Data protection and online privacy (Your Europe)
sources.quote: These rules apply to both companies and organisations (public and private) in the EU and those based outside the EU who offer goods or services in the EU , such as Facebook or Amazon, whenever these companies request or re-use the personal data of individuals in the EU.

L6_consumer_ecommerce.question: Consumer-protection / e-commerce rules for online sales (refunds, disclosures)
L6_consumer_ecommerce.answer: EU consumer law gives a 14-day withdrawal right for online and distance purchases without justification: 14 days from delivery for goods, and from conclusion of the contract for services. Exceptions include personalised goods, perishables and date-specific services.

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: This means you can cancel the contract within 14 days without providing any justification (the "cooling-off period").

sources.title: Returns and the right of withdrawal (Your Europe)
sources.quote: For goods this means 14 days from the date of delivery, for services 14 days after the day the contract was agreed.

L7_incentives.question: Legal incentives / tax holidays / special zones relevant to small digital businesses
L7_incentives.answer: Kleinunternehmerregelung (see L4): VAT-free invoicing for turnover of at most EUR 25,000 in the prior year and EUR 100,000 in the current year, with no input-VAT recovery. An EU-wide small-business scheme also lets German small businesses use exemptions in other member states under conditions. The statute is § 19 UStG (Besteuerung der Kleinunternehmer).

W1_workarounds.question: Simple, legal routes around payment barriers for a beginner (no misrepresentation, nominees or sanctions evasion)
W1_workarounds.answer: Barriers: none of the major platform barriers apply. Simple legal routes: (1) Sell digital products or software through a merchant of record: Paddle (software/SaaS only; each seller reviewed), Lemon Squeezy (bank payouts), Polar, Dodo Payments. The platform is the legal seller to your customers, handles card payments and consumer VAT/sales tax, and pays you out. You still declare the payouts as your income at home (see L3). (2) Sell services on Upwork, which is available here (not on its restricted list). Which withdrawal methods you get (bank, PayPal, Payoneer, etc.) depends on the country and shows in your account. (3) Creator income through the YouTube Partner Program (available here). (4) Paid apps and in-app sales through Google Play (merchant registration available here). (5) Physical or digital goods on Etsy (Etsy seller payments are available here). (6) Client payments by PayPal (on PayPal's Payouts list as 'Fully localized'). (7) Stripe accepts merchants here, so you can take card payments directly on your own site. (8) For direct clients, a bank transfer (SWIFT) into your own local account always works. Follow the local foreign-exchange rules (see P1) and keep invoices. Avoid: opening accounts with a foreign address, a relative's or friend's identity, or a VPN to look like you are elsewhere. It breaches platform terms (accounts and funds get frozen) and can break anti-money-laundering or sanctions law.
